paper_a.title: Another proof of the corona theorem

paper_b.title: A new Proof of the Corona Problem

metadata.description: Both papers prove Carleson's corona theorem on the unit disc but via fundamentally different routes. Tanaka (paper A) derives it as a corollary of a strong cluster-value theorem proved via analytic discs, Hoffman maps, thin interpolating sequences, representing-measure approximations, and elaborate auxiliary Blaschke-product constructions. Geleta (paper B) gives a short, elementary proof using Rudin's subset-sum lemma and a case-split on the vanishing of the sum $G(z)=\sum f_k$, explicitly avoiding Carleson measures and $\bar{\partial}$-techniques. The shared mathematical statement (Bezout form of corona) and the contrast in proof technique make this a clean alternative-proof (AP) pair.

matches.explanation: Both define the algebra $H^\infty$ of bounded analytic functions on the unit disc and its maximal ideal space, with the disc embedded via point-evaluation. Paper A bundles algebra and maximal-ideal space into one foundational definition (DP428.1); paper B splits them across two atomic definitions (DP430.1 for the algebra, DP430.2 for the spectrum/maximal-ideal space). The mathematical content matches exactly.

Paper B explicitly defines the 'corona' as the complement $\mathbb{S}\setminus\overline{\mathbb{D}}$, attributing the term to Newman (1959). Paper A works with the same object implicitly through fiber/closure considerations but never names a 'corona' definition node; the closest concept appears inside lemmas about $X\subset\overline{\Delta}$. Paper-original Level-1 definition with no L1 counterpart.

Paper A's definition of the fiber $\mathfrak{M}_\alpha$ over a boundary point $\alpha\in\mathbf{T}$ is essential to its cluster-value framework. Paper B does not introduce fibers — its proof is purely pointwise on $\mathbb{D}$ and never decomposes the maximal ideal space by boundary points.
Paper A defines cluster sets ${\it Cl}(f,\alpha)$ to formulate the cluster value theorem, the centerpiece of its proof strategy. Paper B has no cluster-set apparatus.

Paper A's basic neighborhood $W(\phi,f_1,\dots,f_N,\varepsilon)$ in the maximal ideal space is used for the density/closure arguments (Lemmas 2.1, 2.3) underpinning the corona deduction. Paper B's proof never works in the topology of $\mathbb{S}$ at this level.
Pseudo-hyperbolic distance is specific to paper A's analytic-discs / Gleason-parts machinery; paper B has no analogue.
Gleason parts and analytic discs are paper-A-specific machinery. Paper B avoids any maximal-ideal-space geometry beyond stating density.
Interpolating / thin sequences are a core ingredient of paper A's Hoffman-map construction; paper B does not invoke interpolation theory.
Interpolating Blaschke products are central to paper A's construction (used in Lemmas 2.2, 4.x, 5.1). Paper B uses no Blaschke products of any kind.
Hoffman maps are paper A's principal tool for embedding the disc into Gleason parts; paper B has no analogue.
The orthogonal-arc mid-point $c$ is a technical construction inside paper A's Lemma 3.3 / Möbius change-of-variables. Paper B uses no boundary-arc geometry.
Sectors $S[s,t)$ index the auxiliary Blaschke construction in paper A's Section 4. No counterpart in paper B.
The algebra $(SB)(\mathfrak{F}^\sharp)$ is bespoke to paper A's normal-families argument in Section 5. Paper B's proof has no algebra of this kind.

Both state Carleson's corona theorem in Bezout form: given $f_1,\dots,f_N\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ with $\sum|f_k|\ge\delta>0$, there exist $g_1,\dots,g_N\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ with $\sum f_k g_k\equiv 1$. The hypotheses, conclusions, and tags align verbatim. Paper A labels it a corollary (of its Theorem TP428.2), while paper B states it as the main theorem — this difference in role does not affect statement-level equivalence.

Paper B factors the corona theorem into a problem statement (ProbP430.1, the Bezout question) plus its theorem (TP430.2, the affirmative answer). Paper A's CP428.1 fuses the question and answer into a single corollary statement. This many-to-one alignment captures that the corona corollary contains both the problem and its resolution.

Tanaka's strong cluster value theorem (existence of a sequence $\zeta_j\to 1$ with $f(\zeta_j)\to f(\phi)$ on a countably-generated subalgebra $B(\mathfrak{F})$, for every $\phi\in\mathfrak{M}_1$) is the principal new contribution of paper A. It strictly generalizes the cluster value theorem and directly implies corona via density. Paper B has no analogous cluster-value statement; the corona theorem is reached without ever proving such a sequence exists. This is the key Level-1 paper-original node with no B-counterpart.
Paper A's Lemma 2.1 (Shilov boundary $X\subset\overline{\Delta}$) is a structural reduction specific to its representing-measure approach. Paper B never localises to a Shilov boundary.
Lemma 2.2 (homeomorphic analytic discs from thin interpolating sequences) is a Hoffman-map result with no analogue in paper B's proof.

Lemma 2.3 is paper A's bridge from finite to countable function families and the iff characterization of $\overline{\Delta}$. Paper B's argument is finite-dimensional throughout (fixed $f_1,\dots,f_N$).

Lemmas 3.1–3.2 (simple-function approximations to $\phi$, then refinement to algebras over $\mathfrak{F}^\sharp$) constitute the representing-measure machinery used in paper A's Section 3. Paper B uses no representing measures.
Möbius change-of-variables Lemma 3.3 is technical scaffolding for paper A's integral computations. Paper B does no change-of-variables.

All four Section-4 lemmas (Blaschke product lower bound, $B\circ L_c$ is Blaschke, construction of $B$ with $B\circ L_{n_j}\to G$, boundary convergence) build the auxiliary Blaschke product central to paper A's proof. Paper B uses no Blaschke products at all — this entire block is paper-A-specific.
Lemma 5.1 (limit identities and polynomial approximation of $H$) is the technical heart of paper A's normal-families step. No counterpart in paper B.

Paper B's Lemma 3.2 — the pointwise functional version of Rudin's subset-sum lemma — is the linchpin of its proof: for every $z$ there exists a subset $S$ with $|\sum_{k\in S}f_k(z)|\ge\frac{1}{\pi}\sum|f_k(z)|$. Paper A's proof never invokes such a subset-sum / averaging principle. This is the key Level-1 paper-original lemma in B with no A-counterpart, and it crystallises why the two proofs are technically disjoint.

Paper B's Theorem 3.3 (subset nonvanishing: a subset $S$ with $\sum_{k\in S}f_k(z)\ne 0$ exists at every $z\in\mathbb{D}$) is the immediate consequence of Lemma 3.2 used to bypass zeros of $\sum f_k$. Paper A has no such subset-selection result; its corona deduction goes via density of $\Delta$ in $\mathfrak{M}(H^\infty)$ instead.
Paper B explicitly raises an open problem (corona for general planar / higher-dimensional domains, citing Cole's counterexample). Paper A makes no such open problem statement.

Both are the proofs of the corona theorem itself, but the techniques are fundamentally different. Paper A's PP428.12 derives corona by reducing 'Bezout solvable' to 'density of $\Delta$ in $\mathfrak{M}(H^\infty)$' and invoking the strong cluster value theorem TP428.2; the heavy lifting is offloaded to PP428.11 and the entire Sections 2–5 apparatus. Paper B's PP430.3 case-splits on whether $G(z)=\sum f_k$ vanishes and constructs the $g_k$ explicitly via $1/G$ on a subset $S$ given by Theorem 3.3. Same theorem proved, totally different proof — the AP relationship is concentrated here.

Paper A's main proof — combining Lemmas 3.1–3.3, 4.3–4.4 and 5.1 to conclude the strong cluster value theorem — has no analogue in paper B because paper B does not prove (or need) any such cluster-value statement.

All ten proof nodes for paper A's auxiliary Lemmas 2.1–5.1 are part of the cluster-value / Hoffman-map / Blaschke-construction machinery. Paper B has no auxiliary lemmas of comparable mathematical content; its single short proof (PP430.3) plus the Rudin-lemma proof (PP430.1) covers everything. Grouped into one composite none entry to keep the alignment compact.

Paper B's proofs of its functional Rudin lemma (PP430.1) and the subset-nonvanishing theorem (PP430.2) have no counterpart in paper A. The Rudin pointwise / subset-sum machinery is entirely absent from paper A's proof strategy.

Paper A's cluster-value identity ${\it Cl}(f,\alpha)=f(\mathfrak{M}_\alpha)$ has no equation-level counterpart in paper B. (Equations are not strictly required to receive none entries under the rules, but listing this here makes the paper-A side complete since it is paper-original Level-1.)
Convergence statement \eqref{eq1.2} is internal to paper A's cluster-value formulation; no B counterpart.
Möbius-map definition $L_n(\zeta)=(\zeta+c_n)/(1+\overline{c_n}\zeta)$ is paper A's Hoffman-map ingredient; paper B uses no Möbius transformations.
Halving and sign-decomposition identities are technical equations in Section 3 of paper A; no analogue in paper B.
Representation $h(\phi)=H(0)=\int H\,dm$ is the central identity of paper A's Section 5 proof. Paper B has nothing comparable.

Paper B's corona lower-bound condition $\sum|f_k|>\delta>0$ appears verbatim inside paper A's CP428.1 statement (matched above). Listing this equation match for completeness; both papers articulate the same hypothesis.
Paper B's Bezout identity equation $\sum f_k g_k = 1$ matches the conclusion of paper A's corona corollary CP428.1 exactly. Listed at equation level for completeness.
Paper B explicitly notes the trivial nonanalytic Bezout solution $g_k=\bar{f}_k/\sum|f_j|^2$ to motivate the difficulty. Paper A does not surface this observation.

External cited result — classical cluster value theorem (Hoffman 1962). Paper B does not cite it because its proof bypasses cluster-value theory entirely. Listed because it is the direct ancestor of paper A's main theorem and shows the genealogical disconnect from paper B.
External: Newman's theorem on the existence of a Blaschke product vanishing at a point of $\mathfrak{M}(H^\infty)\setminus X$. Used in paper A's Lemma 4.3; not invoked by paper B.
External Wermer embedding theorem; used in paper A's Lemma 2.2 and Remark (a). Not invoked by paper B.
External Hoffman characterization of analytic discs; used in paper A's Section 2. Not invoked by paper B.

External Carleson-measure definition is cited by paper B only to disclaim that its proof avoids Carleson measures (see RP430.2). Paper A also avoids Carleson measures explicitly but does not surface a Carleson-measure node.

Both papers cite a 'classical' theorem from the corona/cluster-value lineage as scene-setting. Paper A cites Hoffman's classical cluster value theorem (TP428.1); paper B cites Carleson's corona theorem itself as the named historical result (TP430.3, the density form $\overline{\mathbb{D}}=\mathbb{S}$). They are not the same external result, but they play parallel roles as the cited prior-art benchmark each paper frames its contribution against. Confidence medium because the underlying cited statements differ (cluster-value vs. corona).

Both papers append a forward-looking remark gesturing at extensions / generalizations beyond the unit disc. Paper A's RP428.2 (sparse $\{\zeta_j\}$ and analytic-disc geometry) and paper B's RP430.1 (extension to bounded planar domains and several variables) are not the same content but occupy the same authorial role. Tagged analogous, medium confidence.

Paper B explicitly remarks that its proof bypasses Carleson measures and $\bar{\partial}$ techniques. Paper A's whole enterprise also avoids those techniques (using analytic-discs / Hoffman maps instead) but never says so as a remark. Listed at low confidence because the meta-claim 'avoids prior corona machinery' is implicit in paper A but explicit in paper B; auxiliary 'remark'-type node so omission is also acceptable, but worth flagging.

Composite L1↔L2 alignment of the two proofs of the corona theorem. Paper A's PP428.12 is one short proof node arguing 'density of $\Delta$ in $\mathfrak{M}(H^\infty)$ implies corona', which is essentially a one-step deduction from TP428.2. Paper B unfolds its corona proof into four atomic steps PSP430.1–PSP430.4: (1) easy zero-free case; (2) general case via Theorem 3.3; (3) define $g_k=1/G$ on $S$, $0$ off $S$; (4) verify the Bezout identity. The composite alignment captures that paper B's step decomposition is the operational substance of its proof, while paper A's corona deduction is essentially trivial once TP428.2 is in hand. Justifies the AP classification: same theorem, structurally different proofs.
